analysis.one_liner: Bans PAC money in House races, caps campaign spending, and shuts down unlimited party soft money.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on it: the Campaign Finance System Reform Act was referred to the House Administration Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there until the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten campaign finance rules for House elections. It banned House candidates from taking money from political action committees (PACs) and from anyone who did not live in their own district, set a $600,000 cap on campaign spending, and required all party money spent on federal elections — including 'soft money', the unlimited contributions parties raised outside the normal limits — to follow federal limits and be publicly reported. It also tightened the rules on what counts as a supposedly 'independent' campaign expenditure and barred using government aircraft for campaign travel.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and candidates who lack access to big money. Banning PAC contributions and outside-district money would force House candidates to rely on many small donations from the people they represent, and spending caps would lower the price of running a competitive campaign — which tends to help challengers take on well-funded incumbents. Requiring party soft money to be publicly reported would let voters see who was bankrolling party activity.

how_it_helps.text: Banned House candidates from accepting any contribution from a multicandidate PAC or any other source except individuals [S2][S3].
Required House candidates to accept contributions only from individual residents of their own congressional district [S2][S3].

Set a $600,000 cap on an eligible House candidate's spending per election cycle, with allowances for runoff and special elections, and capped personal contributions from a candidate's own funds at $50,000 [S3].

Made any party money raised or spent 'directly or indirectly' in connection with a federal election — including soft money — fully subject to federal limits, prohibitions, and reporting, and prohibited national party committees from soliciting unlimited contributions [S2][S3].

Required national and state party committees to report all receipts and disbursements, whether or not connected to a federal election, and expanded reporting of exempt contributions and expenditures [S3].
Narrowed the definition of 'independent expenditure' to treat spending coordinated with a candidate as a regulated contribution, closing a route around contribution limits [S2][S3].
Prohibited using government-owned or -operated aircraft in connection with federal elections, except for presidential travel, whose campaign-related cost the campaign must pay [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees, which would lose their ability to give to House candidates; big-dollar and out-of-district donors; and party committees that raise unlimited soft money. Incumbents and challengers who rely on PAC funding would have to rebuild their fundraising around individual donors.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, big donors, and party soft-money operations

drawbacks.text: The district-resident rule (Sec. 102) would bar House candidates from accepting money from supporters who live elsewhere in the state or country, cutting off some legitimate donors [S3].

The spending cap applies only to candidates who opt in; under the bill's own 'nonparticipating opponent' provisions, the limits disappear if an opponent refuses to comply and spends past a threshold, so a wealthy self-funder or outside-funded rival could make the limits meaningless [S3].

Expenditure caps like these have faced constitutional challenge as limits on political speech, and the bill's very low compliance burden exceptions (fundraising costs, legal and accounting costs) create paperwork and gray areas [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: capping PAC money, outside-district money, and party soft money would make House elections cheaper and more accountable to local voters, at the cost of cutting off some voluntary donors and creating enforceability problems when one side refuses the limits. The bill's carve-outs and opt-in structure are weaknesses an honest supporter would acknowledge, but the substance is a genuine anti-big-money reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry Costello introduced the bill on January 6, 1993 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration [S5].
That was the last action of any kind; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs, big-dollar donors, and party soft-money operations kept the fundraising system unchanged, since the bill never even received a hearing. Nothing in the record shows committee leadership ever scheduled action on it.

for.name: Rep. Jerry F. Costello
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Campaign Finance System Reform Act on January 6, 1993

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 103rd Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 6, 1993 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The sponsor was a Democrat and the two cosponsors split one Republican and one Democrat, so the bill's tiny base was bipartisan, but the committee that buried it was run by the majority party.

industries.note: PACs exist to pool big-money contributions and deliver them to candidates; the bill would have banned PAC money in House races outright (Sec. 101). Their interest in the existing system runs against voters who want campaigns funded by small individual donors.

The bill would have made all party money spent in connection with federal elections subject to federal limits and reporting, and barred national committees from soliciting unlimited contributions (Sec. 202). Soft money was the parties' largest unregulated funding channel.

Spending caps and fundraising restrictions would shrink the money flowing through the campaign industry, though fundraising-cost exemptions and new compliance and reporting duties create some paid work (Secs. 501(f), 502(f), 204).

industries.industry: Lobbying community and large corporate donors
industries.note: Restricting contributions to in-district individuals and tightening the coordination rules on 'independent' spending would reduce the leverage of large donors trying to buy access to House members.
